items.label: Hacker News
items.title: Show HN: bouncemarket – a live prediction market game for a bouncing ball
items.body:
a ball will fall. trade on where it lands.

I made this game! Some technical details:

The entire drop of the ball is simulated server-side, then streamed to each client as server-sent events with a small buffer. Every drop is deterministic from its starting position, so rounds can be replayed exactly for later analysis, but tiny variations in starting position can change the ultimate outcome.

There's some AI traders to keep the market moving, but they drop out in any round that has more than five people. They operate using a naive set of rules that I wrote for them, so they're not too hard to beat -- it's when the market is full of real people that it gets tricky.

Curious to get feedback on anything you would change, and especially whether the mechanics were clear right away or not.

---

items.body:
Rad Pro, a [custom firmware for Geiger counters/radiation meters](https://github.com/Gissio/radpro), has a random number generator. It is a [Hardware Random Number Generator](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Hardware_random_number_generator), it generates random numbers from a physical process (radiation).

From the main screen:

![](https://blog.didierstevens.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/image-8.png)

You go into the settings menu to Random generator:

![](https://blog.didierstevens.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/image-9.png)

And there you have many options:

![](https://blog.didierstevens.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/image-10.png)

I select Alphanumeric, and this gives me a random string:

![](https://blog.didierstevens.com/wp-content/uploads/2026/11/image-11.png)

You can see the string grow while radiation is detected. It’s slow with normal background radiation, it takes several seconds for a new character to appear. It’s not practical if you need a lot of random data.

items.body:
*This essay originally appeared in [The Guardian](https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfree/2026/nov/20/cyber-attacks-outages-blame-economy). It’s an expanded version of the one I posted as “[We Get the Infrastructure We Pay For](https://www.schneier.com/blog/archives/2026/11/we-get-the-infrastructure-we-pay-for.html).”*

It’s been a bad week for our computerized infrastructure. We’ve seen outages at [Microsoft](https://www.the-independent.com/tech/microsoft-outage-why-what-caused-global-outlook-down-b3085576.html), the [FAA](https://www.nytimes.com/2026/11/15/us/router-network-faa-airline-ground-stop.html), a handful of [banks](https://apnews.com/article/bank-outage-chase-wells-fargo-truist-50fee2693c22f597fa6ca51a97ef2cda), [United Airlines](https://www.nbcnews.com/news/us-news/united-airlines-system-outage-rcna609712), an unnamed classified [NSA network](https://www.reuters.com/technology/highly-classified-us-national-security-communications-network-is-down-cnn-2026-11-17/), and [Apple](https://www.digitaltrends.com/phones/apple-services-hit-by-widespread-outage-reports-users-flag-problems-with-icloud-app-store-and-apple-pay/). People should be forgiven for suspecting a coordinated cyberattack, a common cause, or at least a conspiracy. But there is none.

The incidents are unrelated. They’re not the result of any cyberattack, coordinated or not. And, even more surprising, they don’t seem to be the result of AI. (We can’t say anything about the NSA; we’ll probably never know the details of that one.) It’s really just a series of unfortunate coincidences.

None of them should surprise, though. Our computerized infrastructure is both vulnerable and fragile.

Much of it is old and has been incrementally patched and upgraded over the decades. A surprising amount of it is maintained by hobbyists, without any recompense. There often aren’t good backup systems. And more and more of it is centralized, meaning that individual failures have cascading consequences across many different aspects of our lives and society.

A lot of our tech infrastructure just barely works. And when it fails, it can fail badly. It’s the very opposite of resilience.

There are a lot of technological reasons why this is true, but they are all downstream from the economic ones. The technologies we rely on are built and maintained within our economic system—and that’s where the core problems lie.

Security, safety, resilience, redundancy and recoverability are all essential parts of reliable technology, but they are all costs. More importantly, they are costs that don’t generate near-term profits.

Modern shareholder capitalism, and private equity in particular, prioritizes near-term profits over everything else. This squeezes all apparent inefficiencies—and, additionally, all other positive intangibles—out of a company in pursuit of those profits.

Market competition, essential for the forces that nudge companies to provide better services, is another perceived inefficiency. Monopolization removes it in pursuit of near-term profits.

From the perspective of a quarterly budget, spending on reliability measures is an inefficiency. They’re expenses that don’t generate revenue. They feel wasteful  until something bad happens.

But, if you’re lucky, you can push the costs of failure on to society, further increasing profits. So, we get stranded in airports when planes don’t fly, or have to deal with the fallout when we can’t withdraw money from our bank accounts.

The effects of those economic pressures are brittle systems, with single points of failure and cascading failure modes. They’re more susceptible to cyberattack—both human and AI-fueled—and more susceptible to random mistakes.

The more we allow unregulated capitalism to privatize gains while socializing risks, the more we should expect these sorts of failures.

Upgrading our computerized systems, increasing their reliability, removing single points of failure, and making them more resilient are all technical problems. But they won’t happen until we fix the political and economic ones.

We need to change the economic incentives that make it profitable to operate these systems just at the edge of functionality, and to push the costs of failure on to all of us. Fixing that requires regulation—with enforcement and meaningful fines—and stringent antitrust enforcement.

But while that’s all easy to say, it’s much harder to [implement](https://www.thenation.com/article/politics/make-america-function-again/)—especially in the US where monied interests have such a tight hold on the legislative agenda. Until this changes, we should expect lots more of these sorts of failures in the future.
